questions.q: Why can a notebook "work" when run interactively but fail to reproduce when run fresh from top to bottom?
options: Jupyter corrupts .ipynb files after too many edits
The kernel retains variables in memory from cells that were later edited, reordered, or deleted, so the visible cell order no longer matches the actual execution history
Jupyter notebooks cannot contain more than 50 cells
pandas behaves differently inside a notebook than in a script
questions.explain: A notebook's kernel keeps whatever state resulted from the actual order cells were run in, which can diverge from the order cells appear in on disk once cells are edited, reordered, or deleted -- producing results that only reproduce in that specific kernel session.

questions.q: Why are .ipynb files particularly unfriendly to git diffs and merges?
options: Git cannot track files with a .ipynb extension at all
The file is JSON containing code, markdown, and cell outputs (including embedded image data), so diffs are dominated by execution counters and re-rendered output rather than the actual logic change
Jupyter notebooks are stored as encrypted binary files
nbconvert must be run before every git commit
questions.explain: An .ipynb file bundles code with every cell's output, including base64-encoded plot images, so a small logic change produces a diff full of unrelated output noise, and real merge conflicts in that JSON are painful to resolve by hand.

questions.q: What does `papermill` add on top of what `nbconvert --execute` already does?
options: It converts a notebook directly into a PDF with no code execution
It deletes all outputs from a notebook before saving it
It executes a notebook as a parameterized batch job, injecting different parameter values into a designated cell on each run
It replaces the Jupyter kernel with a faster interpreter
questions.explain: papermill re-runs a notebook with parameters injected into a parameters cell (e.g. a different universe or lookback each run), turning a one-off notebook into a repeatable, parameterized job -- nbconvert alone just re-executes or converts the notebook as-is.

questions.q: In the lesson's `momentum_signal` example, what is the purpose of moving the function out of the notebook and into `signal_lib.py` with a test?
options: Functions run faster when defined in a separate file
pandas requires functions to be defined outside notebooks to work correctly
It lets the notebook keep doing fast exploratory work while the logic that's actually relied upon lives somewhere a test suite protects it from silent breakage
It is required before a notebook can produce any plots
questions.explain: The graduation pattern keeps the notebook as a disposable exploration space while logic that other code now depends on moves into a tested module, so a regression in that logic gets caught by the test suite rather than discovered later.

questions.q: What is the standard check for whether a notebook is actually reproducible, not just working in the current session?
options: Checking that the notebook file size is under 1MB
Restarting the kernel and running all cells top to bottom (Restart & Run All)
Counting the number of markdown cells
Opening the notebook in a different web browser
questions.explain: Restart & Run All clears all kernel state and re-executes every cell in the order they appear on disk, which is the only reliable way to confirm the notebook doesn't depend on hidden state from a different execution order.
